Faithful Servant
FAYTH-ful SUR-vant
noun phrase (the steward of the parables)
From the Authorized Version; the “good and faithful servant” commended by the lord in the parables of stewardship and watchfulness.

📖 Biblical Definition

The faithful servant is the figure, drawn from our Lord's parables, of the steward who is found at his Master's return doing the work entrusted to him, and who hears the great commendation, “Well done, thou good and faithful servant… enter thou into the joy of thy lord.” In the parable of the talents the faithful servants traded with what they were given and rendered the increase; the wicked servant buried his talent and was cast out. In the parable of the watchful steward the question is asked, “Who then is a faithful and wise servant, whom his lord hath made ruler over his household, to give them meat in due season?”—and blessed is that servant whom his lord, when he cometh, shall find so doing. The standard is not the size of the gift but the fidelity of the steward: it is required in stewards that a man be found faithful, and he that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much. The dictionary marks the faithful servant against the corruption that measures discipleship by visible greatness or success; the Master commends faithfulness, not bigness, and the servant with two talents hears the same “well done” as the servant with five. The figure also guards against the presumption of the wicked servant who said in his heart, “My lord delayeth his coming,” and turned to self-indulgence. The believer is a steward of time, gifts, gospel, and household, who labours in his Master's absence and watches for His sure return, that he may give account with joy.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The steward of the parables found doing his Master's work at His return, who hears “Well done, thou good and faithful servant” (Matthew 25:21); the standard is fidelity, not greatness, watchfulness, not presumption.

expand to see more

FAITHFUL SERVANT, noun phrase. The steward commended at his lord's return for doing the work entrusted to him.

“Well done, thou good and faithful servant… enter thou into the joy of thy lord” (Matthew 25:21).

The faithful and wise servant gives the household meat in due season (Matthew 24:45).

It is required in stewards that a man be found faithful (1 Corinthians 4:2).

The standard is fidelity, not greatness; faithfulness in the least, not the size of the gift.

📖 Key Scripture

Mt 25:21 — "His lord said unto him, Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord."

Mt 24:45 — "Who then is a faithful and wise servant, whom his lord hath made ruler over his household, to give them meat in due season?"

1 Co 4:2 — "Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful."

Lu 16:10 — "He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much: and he that is unjust in the least is unjust also in much."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The success-driven age measures discipleship by visible greatness and results, missing the Master's standard of fidelity in what is least and watchfulness in His absence.

expand to see more

Much modern Christianity, shaped by the metrics of business and celebrity, measures a servant of God by the size of his platform, the numbers of his ministry, the visibility of his gifts. The parables overturn this. The servant with two talents heard the very same “well done” as the servant with five, for the Master commends fidelity, not magnitude. He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much. The dictionary recovers the standard: a faithful servant is not a great one by the world's reckoning but a true one by his Lord's, found doing the work entrusted to his hand.

The opposite corruption is the presumption of the wicked servant who said, “My lord delayeth his coming,” and gave himself to indulgence and the beating of his fellow-servants. The delay of the Master is no proof of His absence; He will come in a day the servant looketh not for him. The dictionary holds the parable's sober edge: the steward labours in his Lord's absence and watches for His sure return, neither despairing at delay nor presuming upon it, that he may render his account with joy and not with grief.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the Greek doulos (bondservant) and pistos (faithful, trustworthy); the steward (oikonomos) is the household manager accountable to his lord.

expand to see more

Doulos, Greek, a bondservant or slave, wholly belonging to his master.

Pistos, Greek, faithful, trustworthy, the quality the master commends.

Oikonomos, Greek, a steward or household manager, accountable for what is entrusted.

Eu, doule agathe kai piste, “well done, good and faithful servant” (Matthew 25:21).

The “talents” and the “meat in due season” figure the gifts and duties of stewardship.

Usage

"The pastor reminded the small congregation that the Master commends faithfulness, not bigness, and the two-talent servant heard the same “well done.”"

"He warned against the servant who presumed upon his lord's delay and turned to self-indulgence."

"She sought to be faithful in the least things, knowing that fidelity there is the proof of fidelity in much."
